learningObjective: Precisely characterize the defining property of SSA (Static Single Assignment) form and distinguish it from related notions.

canonicalClaims.claim: SSA is a syntactic IR property: each variable name has exactly one textual definition, and φ-functions at control-flow join points merge reaching definitions from predecessor blocks.
conditions: The IR admits a well-formed CFG.
Loops introduce φ-functions at loop headers to merge initial and backedge values.
nonImplications: Does not imply φ-functions have runtime cost.
Does not imply loops must be unrolled to satisfy SSA.

misconceptions.claim: SSA prohibits loops because a variable would be written on each iteration.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SSA is a textual property; a loop header uses a single φ-function to merge the initial value and the backedge value.

misconceptions.claim: SSA is a memory-layout property enforced by the register allocator.
misconceptions.whyWrong: SSA is an IR-level syntactic property; register allocation typically operates after out-of-SSA translation.

misconceptions.claim: SSA variables must be compile-time constants.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Single assignment refers to a single textual definition; the assigned expression can be a runtime-computed value.

implementationFacts: Cytron et al. algorithm places φ-functions using dominance frontiers.
Out-of-SSA translation inserts copies at predecessor blocks to eliminate φ-functions.
LLVM, MLIR, and modern compilers use SSA-based IRs.
performanceScenarios: SSA simplifies constant propagation, dead-code elimination, and value numbering by making def-use relationships explicit.
